
Reading the plate offense first, then defense, is deliberate: it is the order of the checklist. Offensive
tells belong to step 3, when everyone is set; defensive tells to steps 6 to 8, when the defense has settled
(or pretended to). Two of the stance tells are easier to understand from the side:

```{python}
#| label: fig-stance-pairs
#| fig-cap: "Two stance tells seen from the side (the line of scrimmage is to the right; the dot and arrow mark where the weight is). A and B: a tackle about to drive forward stands square, shoulders over a heavy hand; a tackle about to kick back into his pass set staggers his outside foot well back and sits on it. C and D: a tight end in a three-point stance on the line is set up to block (though a good one releases from the same stance); one standing up a yard off the line is set up to get into a route quickly. The tight end tell is weaker: many teams put the tight end in a two-point stance on every snap."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.15))
blank(ax)
ax.set_xlim(0, 44)
ax.set_ylim(-5.2, 11.0)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.plot([0.5, 43.5], [2, 2], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2)
LW = 2.6
WEIGHT = style.DEFENSE_DARK


def stick(x0, pts, head, col=style.OFFENSE):
    fb, ff, kb, kf, hip, sh, hand = pts
    for a, b in ((fb, kb), (kb, hip), (ff, kf), (kf, hip), (hip, sh), (sh, hand)):
        ax.plot([x0 + a[0], x0 + b[0]], [a[1], b[1]], color=col, lw=LW, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x0 + head[0], head[1]), 0.85, fc=col, ec="none"))


def weight(x, y):
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.42, fc=WEIGHT, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=5))
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x, y + 0.5), xytext=(x, y + 2.3), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=WEIGHT, lw=1.3),
                zorder=5)


# A: tackle, heavy three-point, feet square
stick(5.5, [(-2.0, 2), (0.3, 2), (-1.3, 4.0), (1.0, 3.8), (-1.3, 5.9), (2.8, 5.4), (2.1, 2.15)], (3.7, 5.9))
weight(5.5 + 2.1, 1.75)
# B: tackle, pass set coming: outside foot far back, hips down, hands up, weight on the back foot
stick(16.0, [(-3.6, 2), (0.6, 2), (-2.6, 4.2), (1.1, 4.3), (-1.7, 6.0), (0.2, 8.0), (1.9, 6.6)], (0.6, 9.0))
weight(16.0 - 3.6, 1.75)
# C: tight end, three-point on the line
stick(27.0, [(-2.3, 2), (0.1, 2), (-1.5, 4.1), (0.8, 4.0), (-1.7, 6.4), (2.2, 6.6), (2.0, 2.15)], (3.2, 7.2))
weight(27.0 - 0.9, 1.75)
# D: tight end, two-point, a yard off the line
stick(37.0, [(-1.8, 2), (0.8, 2), (-1.2, 4.3), (1.2, 4.2), (-0.6, 6.0), (0.6, 8.4), (1.5, 6.8)], (1.0, 9.3))
weight(37.0 + 0.8, 1.75)
for d_ in (22.0, 43.0):
    ax.plot([d_, d_], [2.0, 8.6], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
    ax.text(d_ - 0.4, 9.3, "line ►", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
for x_, t in ((6.0, "A  tackle, square,\nheavy hand → run block?"),
              (15.5, "B  tackle, outside foot\nback → pass set?"),
              (27.0, "C  tight end, hand down\non the line → block?"),
              (37.5, "D  tight end, standing\noff the line → route?")):
    ax.text(x_, 0.9, t, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK, linespacing=1.12)
plt.show()
```

Here is the whole catalogue as a reference table: what each tell usually means, *why* it leaks (a tell
that has no physical or tactical reason behind it won't survive a self-scout), how much to trust it, and
whether you'll see it live or only on the replay.

| # | Tell | Usually means | Why it leaks | How far to trust it; where you'll see it |
|:-|:--------|:------------------|:--------------|:-------------|
| 1 | Linemen's stance and weight | Heavy hand, weight forward: run. Light hand, hips back, a tackle's outside foot staggered: pass | A 320-pound man can't explode forward from his heels or kick back from his fingertips | Medium on early downs; quiet on short yardage, when everyone is heavy. *Replay (end zone); live only on close-ups.* |
| 2 | Back's depth and offset | Shotgun runs usually cross the quarterback's face, away from the back's side; a deeper back wants time to read | The handoff path points one way; reading blocks needs a running start | Medium for direction; weak for run or pass. *Live, every snap.* |
| 3 | Shotgun, pistol or under center | Shotgun mostly pass (`{python} pct(RATE["gun"])` in 2025); pistol and under center mostly run | Each alignment is built for a family of plays | Strong for run/pass, but under-center passes are mostly play-action, built to exploit this tell. *Live, every snap.* |
| 4 | Receiver split | Reduced: a crack block, a short crosser, or room to break outside. Wide: an isolated route, deep or breaking inside | Receivers set their split to make their job easier | Weak: tells you *where* to look more than *what*. *Live on the wide shot; replay otherwise.* |
| 5 | Tight end's stance | Hand down on the line: block likely. Standing, flexed: route likely | Blocking starts low; releasing starts tall | Weak; many teams stand the tight end up on every snap. *Live.* |
| 6 | Defensive lineman's width and stance | Wide-aligned edge: pass rush. A lineman sitting back: stunt or drop | A wide rusher has a straight path to the quarterback; a looper needs his weight back | Medium on obvious passing downs. *Replay; live from the end-zone shot.* |
| 7 | Linebacker depth | Creeping to 3 yards late: blitz or a downhill run fit. Backing out early: zone drop | A blitzer needs a head start; a dropper needs depth | Medium; walking up is also a bluff. *Live, on the wide shot.* |
| 8 | Nickel's spot | Apexed: run support or zone. Tight on the slot: man, or a nickel blitz | Man coverage needs proximity; an apex keeps both jobs in reach | Medium. *Live.* |
| 9 | Corner depth and leverage | Press: man or a hard corner. Off with outside leverage: help inside (a deep middle safety). Inside leverage: help outside or over the top | A defender takes away the side where he has no help | Medium; leverage also follows the play-call's coverage of the week. *Replay (skycam); live on the wide shot.* |
| 10 | Safety depth and width | Deep on the hash or outside it: a deep half or quarter. The shallower, narrower or moving one: the rotation | A safety can't cover more than about eight to ten yards of ground between the snap and the throw | Strong *when it moves late*; disguise is the norm. *Top edge of the TV picture; skycam replay.* |

A few of these deserve a sentence more than the table can give them.

**The back's offset is a direction tell, not a run-or-pass tell.** Shotgun runs most often send the back
across the quarterback's face, because the mesh (the moment the ball is handed off) happens while the back is
moving across. A back offset to the right usually runs left. But the same offset is where a back sets up
to pass-protect against a rusher from that side, so it tells you *which way* a run goes far more than
*whether* there will be one.

**The split tell has two readings, and the book has given you both.** A reduced split brings a receiver
closer to the formation, which helps three different jobs: a [crack block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block)
on a linebacker or safety inside him, a short crossing route (the trip across is shorter), and a route that
breaks *outside* and needs room to get there. That's why [reduced split](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reduced-split)
is a weak tell for *what* is coming. Its real value is a *where*: when a receiver tightens his split on a run
look, watch the defender inside him, because that's the man he's coming to block.

**Leverage points at the help.** A defender usually lines up to take away the side where he has no help,
and funnels the receiver toward the side where he has some. So a corner with outside leverage and a single
safety in the middle is telling you the safety is his help; a corner with inside leverage against two-high
may have a safety over the top and outside. Read leverage as an arrow pointing at the help, and the coverage
family usually follows.

**Safety width is the most underused tell.** Everyone counts deep safeties; few look at how far apart they
are. A two-high safety standing on the hash or outside it has a deep half or deep quarter to cover and can't
reach the deep middle in time. A two-high safety cheated inside the hash, eight yards or fewer from the
middle, *can*, and the one standing shallower than his partner can come down. That asymmetry, not the
two-high picture itself, is how you see a rotation coming.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"NFL players are too good to have tells." Every player has tendencies, because the best way to do a job
quickly is to start in the position the job needs. What separates good teams from bad ones isn't the absence
of tells, it's what they do about them. Every staff [self-scouts](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-self-scout)
its own film looking for the clue an opponent could read, and then decides whether to break it, hide it, or
keep it as bait ([Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)).
The Rams' under-center passing in 2025 is the textbook bait: the alignment says run, so the linebackers step
up, and the play-action pass goes behind them. A tell that is right 70% of the time is still worth using.
You just shouldn't be 95% sure of it.
:::

## Stated confidence: putting a number on it

Step 9 asks for a number, and this is where the course's most important habit gets its name. A
[**stated confidence**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stated-confidence) is the probability you attach to a
prediction before the snap, said or written as a number rather than a feeling: not "probably a pass" but
"pass, 75%." The prediction log has had a confidence column since Part 1. From here on, it is not optional.

Why a number, rather than just the call?

1. **It separates a read from a guess.** A 55% call and a 90% call that both miss are different mistakes.
   The first was honest uncertainty; the second was a misread. Without the number, your log can't tell
   them apart.
2. **It forces you to use the base rate.** You can't say "80%" for a pass on first-and-10 without asking
   what moved you from 50. If nothing did, the honest number is 50 to 55.
3. **It can be scored.** A forecaster who says "70% chance of rain" isn't wrong when it stays dry; she's
   wrong if, across all her 70% days, it rains on nine in ten, or on three in ten. Your calls work the same
   way: a 70% call should come true about seven times in ten. The next chapter,
   [Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd), scores the season's log that way, with a
   [Brier score](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-brier-score) (the average squared gap between your stated
   confidence and what happened) and a [calibration](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-calibration) plot (do
   your 70% calls come true about 70% of the time?). Researchers who study forecasters have found that
   saying the number, rather than a word like "probably", is itself one of the habits that makes forecasters
   better.[^tetlock]

How do you choose the number? Start from the base rate (step 1), move it with the strong clues (the
formation is the big one), and then respect two limits:

- **Never below 50.** Your call is whichever side you think is more likely, so its confidence is at least
  50%. A 50% call is perfectly honest: it says "I have nothing", and logging it is better than skipping the
  snap.
- **Rarely above 90.** Offenses choose when to break their tendencies, and the snaps that break them are the
  ones built to fool you. Even the most lopsided situations in football leave room for a surprise:
  third-and-9 is a pass `{python} pct(RATE["third7"])` of the time, not 100%. A reader who logs 99% will be
  badly wrong once a quarter and will learn nothing from it.

What does a well-judged spread of confidences look like? Here is the model from the previous section
(steps 1 to 3 only: situation, personnel and formation) on every 2025 snap, grouped by how sure it was:

```{python}
#| label: fig-confidence-bands
#| fig-cap: "What honest confidence looks like for run or pass. Every 2025 regular-season run and dropback, grouped by how confident a model using only steps 1 to 3 (situation, personnel, formation; learned on 2024) was in its call. Bars: the share of snaps in each band. Labels: how often the call in that band was right. The calls come true at close to the rate they claim (two to four points less often, because the model learned on a different season), and about one snap in five really is a 90%-plus call (long-yardage downs, empty backfields, the end of halves). The rest are spread across the middle, where most of football lives. Source: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.35))
labs = [f"{int(b['lo'] * 100)}–{int(round(b['hi'] * 100))}%" for b in BANDS]
ys = np.arange(len(BANDS))[::-1]
shades = style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[1:6]
ax.barh(ys, [b["share"] for b in BANDS], color=shades, height=0.62, zorder=2)
for y_, b in zip(ys, BANDS):
    ax.text(b["share"] + 0.006, y_, f"{pct(b['share'])} of snaps  ·  right {pct(b['acc'])}", va="center",
            ha="left", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, labs, fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_ylabel("the model's confidence", fontsize=7.6)
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.52)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("share of 2025 snaps", fontsize=7.6)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

That chart is the target for your own log. When the model says 70 to 80%, it's right
`{python} pct(BANDS[2]["acc"])` of the time; when it says 90% or more, it's right `{python} pct(BANDS[4]["acc"])`
of the time. Nobody expects a person to match a model learned on
33,000 snaps, but the *shape* is the goal: confident where the situation is lopsided, modest everywhere
else, and right about as often as you claimed.[^bands]

A small vocabulary helps you say the number fast:

| Say | Means | Typical use |
|:---------|:-----:|:----------------------------------|
| "Coin flip" | 50% | Nothing to go on: the formation was off screen, or the clues pull both ways |
| "Lean" | 55–60% | First-and-10 from a balanced look; one weak clue |
| "Probably" | 65–70% | The formation agrees with the situation |
| "Likely" | 75–80% | A strong formation clue and a situation that points the same way |
| "Near certain" | 85–90% | Third-and-long, an empty backfield, a two-minute drill when trailing |

### Layered predictions

Run or pass is the first layer, and after step 3 it's mostly decided. A good reader makes a second call on
the snaps where there's time, and states a confidence for it too:

- **On a likely pass:** the coverage family (man or zone; one-high or two-high after the snap), the rush
  (four, or five or more), or where the ball should go (the quick throw, the sticks, a shot).
- **On a likely run:** the direction (to the strength, away from the back's offset, at the light side of
  the box) or the scheme family (zone, if the line steps together; gap, if a guard is set to pull).

Second-layer calls are harder, and your confidence should show it. The base rates help here too. In 2025,
defenses sent five or more rushers on only `{python} pct(RUSH["all"])` of dropbacks (`{python} pct(RUSH["third7"])`
on third-and-7 to 10), so "four rush" is the default until a pressure tell moves you off it. Zone was the
coverage on about `{python} pct(1 - MAN_ALL)` of charted 2025 dropbacks, so "zone" is the default coverage
call; FTN's man-coverage share has jumped around from season to season in a way that looks like a change in
charting rather than in football, so treat that number as rough.[^cov] A second-layer call at 60–70% is a good
call. Few are better than that, and anyone who claims to call coverages at 90% before the snap is either
watching a very predictable defense or not keeping score.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden you pick a play from a menu, and when you're on defense you see the offense's formation and pick
a coverage, all with perfect knowledge of your own call. Watching a real game is the reverse: you know
neither call, and neither does anyone on the field. The quarterback's pre-snap read *is* this checklist, run
by the person with the most at stake, and he gets it wrong often enough that offenses build
[hot routes](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) and post-snap reads for the times he does. So a
probability isn't a hedge. It is the most accurate description of what anyone, including the players,
knows before the snap.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"My 90% call missed, so I was wrong." Not necessarily: one in ten 90% calls *should* miss. You can't judge
a single probabilistic call by its outcome, only a pile of them. That's why the log matters, and why
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) scores a season of calls rather than a play. The mistakes to
look for are patterns: 90% calls that miss one time in three (overconfidence), or a log full of 55% calls
that come true 75% of the time (you know more than you're admitting).
:::

## Film room: one drive, nine snaps

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — the NFC Championship Game"}
**The game:** Rams at Seahawks, NFC Championship Game, January 25, 2026, at Lumen Field. Seattle, the NFC's
top seed (14–3), won 31–27 and two weeks later beat New England 29–13 in Super Bowl LX.[^nfc] In 2025 Seattle's
head coach was Mike Macdonald, its offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak (whose system comes from the Shanahan
family tree; see [Shanahan's Wide Zone Tree](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd)) and its
quarterback Sam Darnold.[^staff]

**The drive:** Seattle had gone up 24–13 early in the third quarter; the Rams answered with a touchdown to make
it 24–20 with 9:45 left in the quarter. After the touchback, Seattle drove 65 yards in nine snaps and scored on
third-and-3 from the Rams' 13, a 13-yard pass to Cooper Kupp, to go up 31–20 with 4:52 left in the third.

**Why this drive:** it has a bit of everything the checklist is for: three different personnel groups, under
center and shotgun, an empty backfield, a screen against a blitz, play-action, a no-huddle snap, two third
downs and a red-zone touchdown, against a defense that played base, nickel and dime and three different
coverage labels.

**The sources:** every pre-snap fact below (personnel, the quarterback's alignment, the number of backs,
motion, tempo, box count, defensive personnel) and every post-snap one (rushers, coverage label, time to
throw) comes from the public charting in nflverse: the play-by-play, the participation file and FTN's
charting.[^drive] The diagrams are typical pictures of what was charted, not the film: the charting doesn't
record exact alignments or the routes of receivers who weren't thrown to.
:::

Here is the drive as your log would record it. The calls weren't made by watching the game. They were made
by rule from the pre-snap columns only, so hindsight can't creep in: the run-or-pass call and its confidence
come from the step 1 to 5 model, fitted on the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons; the coverage and rush calls are
the 2025 base rates for that down, distance, field zone and number of defensive backs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-log
#| fig-cap: "The drive as a prediction log: Seattle's nine snaps from its own 35 to the end zone, NFC Championship Game, third quarter. Situation, offense and defense are the pre-snap facts in the charting (UC = under center; M = motion; NH = no-huddle; box = defenders in the box). The calls were made by rule from those facts alone: run or pass from the checklist model, the 'if pass' layer (coverage family, rushers) from 2025 base rates for the situation and the number of defensive backs. The last two columns score the calls; the pass layer is scored only on dropbacks, because coverage isn't charted on runs. Source: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting, game 2025_21_LA_SEA."
COLS = [("#", 2.4), ("Situation", 8.2), ("Offense shows", 12.0), ("Defense", 6.6), ("Call", 5.6),
        ("If pass", 9.6), ("What happened", 13.0), ("R/P", 4.0), ("Pass layer", 7.4)]


def dpers(n):
    return {4: "base", 5: "nickel", 6: "dime"}.get(int(n), "?") if pd.notna(n) else "?"


def off_txt(row, sep=" · "):
    al = {"U": "UC", "S": "gun", "P": "pistol"}.get(row.qb_location, "?")
    nb = int(row.n_offense_backfield)
    backs = "empty" if nb == 0 else f"{nb} back" + ("s" if nb > 1 else "")
    extra = [w for w, f in (("motion", row.is_motion), ("no-huddle", row.is_no_huddle)) if f]
    return f"{row.pers} · {al} · {backs}" + (sep + ", ".join(extra) if extra else "")


def ordinal(n):
    return {1: "1st", 2: "2nd", 3: "3rd", 4: "4th"}[int(n)]


ROWS = []
for i_, row in DRV.iterrows():
    l2 = "–"
    if row.is_pass:
        l2 = ("✓" if row.cov_hit == 1 else "✗") + "  " + ("✓" if row.rush_hit == 1 else "✗")
    ROWS.append([str(i_ + 1), f"{ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}\n{row.yrdln}", off_txt(row, sep="\n"),
                 f"{dpers(row.dbs)}\nbox {int(row.defenders_in_box)}", f"{row.call}\n{row.conf}%",
                 f"{row.cov_call} {row.cov_conf}%\n{row.rush_call} rush {row.rush_conf}%",
                 "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(row.result, 21)), "✓" if row.hit else "✗", l2])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.75))
blank(ax)
Wt = sum(w for _, w in COLS)
nr = len(ROWS)
RH = 2.15
H = 2.4 + 1.5 + RH * nr + 1.7
ax.set_xlim(0, Wt)
ax.set_ylim(0, H)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), Wt, H, fc="#fbfaf4", ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0))
ax.text(0.8, H - 0.95, "PREDICTION LOG  ·  NFC Championship, Rams at Seahawks  ·  Seattle offense, Q3",
        fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
yh = H - 2.4 - 1.5
x = 0
for name, w in COLS:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, yh), w, 1.5, fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, yh + 0.75, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    x += w
for j, vals in enumerate(ROWS):
    yy = yh - (j + 1) * RH
    x = 0
    for (name, w), v in zip(COLS, vals):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, yy), w, RH, fc="white", ec=style.GRID, lw=0.6))
        col = style.INK
        if name in ("R/P", "Pass layer"):
            col = style.THIRD if v.startswith("✓") else (style.DEFENSE_DARK if v.startswith("✗") else style.INK_2)
        left = name in ("Situation", "Offense shows", "Defense", "If pass", "What happened")
        ax.text(x + 0.45 if left else x + w / 2, yy + RH / 2, v, ha="left" if left else "center", va="center",
                fontsize=5.9, color=col, linespacing=1.15,
                fontweight="bold" if name in ("R/P", "Pass layer", "#", "Call") else "normal")
        x += w
ax.text(0.8, 0.85, f"Run/pass: {N_HIT} of {nr} right.   Pass layer on the {int(DRV.is_pass.sum())} dropbacks: "
        f"coverage {N_COV} of {int(DRV.is_pass.sum())}, rushers {N_RUSH} of {int(DRV.is_pass.sum())}.",
        fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK, va="center")
plt.show()
```

And here is how each call was built, step by step, the way the confidence should move in your head:

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-trace
#| fig-cap: "How the run-or-pass confidence moved through the checklist on each snap of the drive. Each row is one snap. The hollow circle is the probability of a pass from the situation alone; the small dots add personnel, then the formation (quarterback alignment and number of backs), then motion and tempo; the filled marker adds the box count and is the final pre-snap call. The right-hand label is what happened, ticked or crossed against the call. The biggest moves come at the formation step, and the misses are the second-and-1 screen (a coin flip that landed the other way) and snaps 7 and 8, passes from under center with two tight ends, exactly the look offenses use to break the tendency. Model fitted on the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons; source: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
n = len(DRV)
ys = np.arange(n)[::-1]
ax.axvline(0.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(0.5, n - 0.35, "coin flip", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
for y_, (i_, row) in zip(ys, DRV.iterrows()):
    pts = [row[f"p{k}"] for k in range(len(TRACE))]
    ax.plot(pts, [y_] * len(pts), color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter([pts[0]], [y_], s=34, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(pts[1:-1], [y_] * (len(pts) - 2), s=10, color=style.INK_2, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter([pts[-1]], [y_], s=48, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=4)
    ax.text(-0.02, y_, f"{i_ + 1}  {ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}, {row.yrdln}", ha="right", va="center",
            fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
    ok = row.hit
    ax.text(1.02, y_, ("✓ " if ok else "✗ ") + ("pass" if row.is_pass else "run") + f": {row.result}",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, color=style.THIRD if ok else style.DEFENSE_DARK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.1)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("chance of a pass, as the checklist goes on", fontsize=7.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", mfc="white", mec=style.INK_2, ms=5, label="situation only"),
                   Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.INK_2, ms=3, label="+ personnel, formation, motion/tempo"),
                   Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ms=6, label="+ box: the final call")],
          loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.17), ncol=3, fontsize=6.6, frameon=False)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.24, right=0.72, bottom=0.2, top=0.95)
plt.show()
```

And the drive in pictures, one pre-snap look per snap:

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-board
#| fig-cap: "The drive in pictures: a typical pre-snap look for each of the nine snaps, built from what was charted (offensive personnel, quarterback alignment, number of backs, defensive personnel and box count, all exact), with the ball on the right yard line and the yellow line to gain. Everything else is illustrative: the charting doesn't record exact alignments, and for runs the safeties are drawn two-high because the coverage isn't charted on runs. For passes the shell is drawn to match the charted coverage family. The ringed player is the ball carrier or the receiver the ball went to. Offense: blue circles; defense: orange squares."
SNAP_LOOK = {1: ("12_1", 5, 2, "two"), 2: ("12_2", 5, 1, "two"), 3: ("11_1", 4, 1, "two"), 4: ("13_2", 5, 2, "two"),
             5: ("11_0", 4, 2, "one"), 6: ("11_1", 4, 2, "one"), 7: ("12_2", 5, 2, "one"), 8: ("12_1", 5, 2, "one"),
             9: ("11_1L", 4, 2, "two")}
SNAP_RING = {1: "RB", 2: "RB", 3: "H", 4: "RB", 5: "RB", 6: "H", 7: "FB", 8: "X", 9: "H"}


def look_offense(kind):
    if kind == "12_1":
        return offense("ace")
    if kind == "12_2":       # a tight end as an offset H-back (two backs in the backfield)
        return [p_.moved(w=-1.5, pos="TE") if p_.key == "FB" else p_ for p_ in offense("offset_i")]
    if kind == "13_2":       # three tight ends: two in line, one as an H-back; one receiver
        o = [p_ for p_ in offense("ace") if p_.key != "X"]
        return o + [Player("FB", "TE", "off", -4.5, 1.5, label="F")]
    if kind == "11_1":
        return offense("gun_2x2")
    if kind == "11_1L":
        return offense("gun_2x2", strength="left")
    if kind == "11_0":
        return offense("gun_empty")
    raise KeyError(kind)


def look_defense(off, line, lbs, shell, dbs):
    LINE = {4: [-5.8, -2.2, 1.0, 5.8], 5: [-6.2, -2.6, 0.0, 2.6, 6.2]}
    LB = {1: [0.8], 2: [-2.4, 2.4]}
    out = [Player(f"DL{k}", "DT", "def", 1.0, w) for k, w in enumerate(LINE[line])]
    out += [Player(f"LB{k}", "LB", "def", 4.5, w) for k, w in enumerate(LB[lbs])]
    rec = [p_ for p_ in off if p_.pos in ("WR", "TE", "RB") and abs(p_.w) > 6.0]
    left = sorted([p_ for p_ in rec if p_.w < 0], key=lambda p_: p_.w)
    right = sorted([p_ for p_ in rec if p_.w > 0], key=lambda p_: -p_.w)
    out += [Player("CBL", "CB", "def", 7.0, (left[0].w if left else -11.0) - 0.8),
            Player("CBR", "CB", "def", 7.0, (right[0].w if right else 11.0) + 0.8)]
    slots = left[1:] + right[1:]
    for k in range(dbs - 4):
        w = slots[k].w + (0.6 if slots[k].w < 0 else -0.6) if k < len(slots) else (-7.5, 7.5)[k % 2]
        out.append(Player(f"NB{k}", "NB", "def", 5.5, w))
    if shell == "two":
        out += [Player("FS", "FS", "def", 12.5, -8.5), Player("SS", "SS", "def", 12.5, 8.5)]
    else:
        out += [Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.0, 0.0), Player("SS", "SS", "def", 9.0, 8.5)]
    return out


fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(6.5, 5.6))
for k, ax in enumerate(axes.flat, start=1):
    row = D.loc[k]
    kind, line, lbs, shell = SNAP_LOOK[k]
    o = [p_.moved(label="") for p_ in look_offense(kind)]
    dfn = [p_.moved(label="") for p_ in look_defense(o, line, lbs, shell, int(row.dbs))]
    los = 110 - row.yardline_100
    pk = Play(o, dfn, los=los, to_go=int(row.ydstogo))
    pk.highlight(SNAP_RING[k])
    fld = pk.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 15.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    ax.set_title(f"{k} · {ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}, {row.yrdln}", fontsize=7.6, loc="left",
                 color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", pad=2)
    short = off_txt(row).replace("motion", "M").replace("no-huddle", "NH")
    ax.text(0.0, -0.03, short + f"  vs  {dpers(row.dbs)}, box {int(row.defenders_in_box)}",
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=5.9, color=style.INK_2)
    ok = row.hit
    ax.text(0.0, -0.13, f"call {row.call.lower()} {row.conf}%  →  {row.result}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="left", va="top", fontsize=5.9, color=style.THIRD if ok else style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.965, bottom=0.07, hspace=0.5, wspace=0.06)
plt.show()
```

Now walk it the way you would live, step by step. The snap numbers match the log.

**Snap 1: first-and-10 at the Seattle 35.** *Situation:* a four-point lead in the third quarter, a coin-flip
down. *Personnel:* 12 (two tight ends); the Rams stay in base. *Formation:* under center, one back, with
motion. Under center with two tight ends on first down is a run look, and the call is
`{python} snap_conf(1)`, only a lean, because Seattle throws from this look too. *Box:* seven defenders against
seven blockers (five linemen, two tight ends), a fair fight. George Holani runs behind the right guard for
three. ✓

**Snap 2: second-and-7.** Second-and-medium leans pass, but Seattle stays in 12 personnel and puts a second
player in the backfield (with one running back and two tight ends on the field, most likely a tight end as an
H-back): two backs, under center. That moves the
call back to `{python} snap_conf(2)`. The Rams answer with a nickel and a six-man box, which is the defense
betting on a pass, and Kenneth Walker loses two yards running around the right end. The call was right; the
run wasn't. That distinction matters for your log: you're scoring your read, not the offense.

**Snap 3: third-and-9 at the 36.** Here the run-or-pass question answers itself (`{python} snap_conf(3)`), and
everything after step 3 goes into the second layer. Seattle goes to 11 personnel in the shotgun; the Rams go
to dime (six defensive backs) with only five men in the box. Six defensive backs and four rushers is a defense
that wants to keep everything in front of it and tackle short of the sticks. The base-rate calls say zone and
a four-man rush, and that's what came: four rushers, and a zone FTN labelled Cover 9 (a number that means
different things to different staffs; see [Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)).
Darnold held the ball 2.8 seconds and found Kupp short, a throw FTN charted as a
checkdown: six yards in the air and six after the catch, a first down by three yards.

```{python}
#| label: fig-snap3
#| fig-cap: "Snap 3, third-and-9 (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun, no motion; the Rams in dime with five in the box; four rushers; a zone labelled Cover 9; a throw after 2.8 seconds to Cooper Kupp (H, ringed) running a quick out on the left, six yards in the air, with six more after the catch for the first down. Illustrative: the alignments, the other routes, and the rotation, drawn as one common meaning of 'Cover 9' (two-high before the snap, the safety away from the tight end coming down, three deep). What to notice: the underneath defenders sink toward the sticks and the quarterback looks right first; the conversion comes from the yards after the catch."
def snap3():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dl = [("OLB1", "OLB", 1.0, -6.6), ("DT1", "DT", 1.0, -2.0), ("DE1", "DE", 1.0, 1.2), ("OLB2", "OLB", 1.0, 6.0)]
    dfn = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in dl]
    dfn += [Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 5.5, 0.6),
            Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 7.5, -15.8, label="CB"), Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.5, 15.8, label="CB"),
            Player("ND", "DB", "def", 6.0, -9.6), Player("DM", "DB", "def", 6.0, 9.6),
            Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.0, -8.5), Player("SS", "SS", "def", 13.0, 8.5)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=46, to_go=9)
    p.highlight("H")
    p.route("X", r.go(13.5)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12)); p.route("Y", r.dig(12, 8))
    p.route("H", r.path((6.5, 0.0), (7.0, 3.5)))           # quick out at about six yards...
    p.route("H", r.path((0.3, 1.0)), speed=0.42)            # ...settles as the checkdown...
    p.route("H", r.path((6.4, 1.6)), speed=6.5)             # ...and turns upfield after the catch
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -0.4)])
    p.dropback(2.5)
    protect(p)
    engage(p, ("OLB1", "DT1", "DE1", "OLB2"))
    # Cover 9 drawn as a weak rotation: the left (weak) safety comes down, the right one runs to the middle
    p.drop("FS", (9.0, -5.0), speed=5.0)
    p.drop("SS", (17.0, 0.0), speed=6.0)
    p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 15.8), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 1.5)); p.drop("DM", (8.5, 11.5))
    p.drop("ND", (8.0, -12.0), speed=4.5)
    p.path("ND", [(12.3, -16.4)], speed=4.2, delay=2.5, absolute=True)   # drives on the throw
    p.read("Z")
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.8)
    return p


s3 = snap3()
animate_or_strip(s3, [0.0, 1.3, 3.8, 4.8],
                 ["Snap · dime, two-high, five in the box", "+1.3 s · three deep; QB looks right",
                  "+3.8 s · the checkdown arrives at six yards", "+4.8 s · twelve yards: past the sticks"],
                 lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.0, 19.5))
```

The lesson of snap 3 is the most common lesson of third-and-long. The run-or-pass call is free; the defense's
plan is easy to read from its personnel (six defensive backs, five in the box: keep it in front, rally,
tackle); and the play is decided by the thing you can't predict, a receiver breaking a tackle or not. Your
second-layer call ("zone, four rush, the ball goes short and the game is the tackle") was right, and that's
as good as reading gets.

**Snap 4: first-and-10 at the 48.** Seattle goes heavy: 13 personnel (three tight ends, one receiver), under
center, two backs, motion. The Rams match with base and *two* nose tackles, a seven-man box. The call is
`{python} snap_conf(4)`, as confident as a first-down run call gets. Walker runs behind the right guard for
eleven. A heavy formation tells you *what*; it doesn't tell you whether it will work.

**Snap 5: first-and-10 at the Rams' 41.** The reverse picture: 11 personnel, shotgun, and **nobody in the
backfield**. An empty backfield is the strongest pass tell in the catalogue (`{python} pct(RATE["empty"])` of
2025 empty-backfield snaps were dropbacks), and the call is `{python} snap_conf(5)`. The second layer is the
interesting part. Empty means five receivers and only five blockers, so a defense that brings a sixth man
gets a free rusher; that's why empty is so often a quick-throw formation. The Rams rushed four and played
Cover 3, and Darnold checked the ball down to Holani, the running back, who had lined up outside the backfield as a receiver, on a
shallow crossing route for nine.

**Snap 6: second-and-1 at the 32.** The most interesting snap of the drive. Second-and-short is the down where
offenses take chances, because even a failed play leaves a manageable third down; from the shotgun with 11
personnel it was a pass `{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11"])` of the time in 2025. The full model, with the
motion and the six-man box added, makes it a coin flip the other way: `{python} snap_conf(6)`. The second layer
said zone (`{python} int(D.loc[6, "cov_conf"])`%) and a four-man rush (`{python} int(D.loc[6, "rush_conf"])`%). The Rams
played zone but sent five, a blitz, and Darnold got the ball out in 0.7 seconds on a screen to Jaxon
Smith-Njigba, who caught it four yards *behind* the line and ran sixteen yards after the catch. ✗ on run or
pass, and a 55% call is allowed to miss: that is what 55% means.

```{python}
#| label: fig-snap6
#| fig-cap: "Snap 6, second-and-1 (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun with motion; the Rams in nickel with six in the box; five rushers (one of them a blitzer) and Cover 3 behind them; a screen to Jaxon Smith-Njigba (H, ringed) on the left, thrown 0.7 seconds after the snap, caught four yards behind the line, sixteen yards after the catch. Illustrative: who motioned (here the tight end, Y, across to the left), which defender blitzed (here the Will linebacker), and the blocks. What to notice: the fifth rusher is a defender who isn't in coverage on the screen side, and the ball is out before he arrives."
def snap6():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = [Player("WDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, -5.8), Player("WDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -2.0),
           Player("SDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, 1.0), Player("SDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 5.8),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.5, 1.8), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 4.5, -2.2),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 5.0, -9.6), Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, -15.8, label="CB"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, 15.8, label="CB"), Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.5, 0.0),
           Player("SS", "SS", "def", 8.5, 9.6)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=78, to_go=1)
    p.highlight("H")
    p.motion("Y", to=(-1.5, -5.6), speed=5.0)                # tight end across: three to the left
    p.motion("SS", to=(8.0, 2.0), speed=3.0)                 # the safety bumps over: a zone answer
    # defense: five rush, Cover 3 behind
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("WILL", speed=5.0)
    p.drop("FS", (14.0, -2.0), speed=3.0)
    p.path("FS", [(12.6, -15.6)], speed=6.0, delay=0.5, absolute=True)
    p.drop("LCB", (10.0, -16.0), speed=3.5)
    p.drop("RCB", (13.0, 15.0), speed=5.0)
    p.path("NB", [(1.5, -11.6)], speed=4.5, absolute=True)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 0.0))
    p.path("MIKE", [(9.0, -10.5)], speed=5.5, delay=0.6, absolute=True)
    p.drop("SS", (8.5, -3.0), speed=4.0)
    # offense: the screen
    protect(p)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.5, 0.4)])
    p.route("H", r.path((-1.5, 1.6), (-2.5, 3.6)), speed=4.0)
    p.route("H", r.path((16.0, 2.4)), speed=7.0)
    p.block("X", target="LCB")
    p.block("Y", target="NB")
    p.route("Z", r.go(14))
    p.dropback(0.8)
    p.pass_to("H", t=0.7)
    return p


s6 = snap6()
animate_or_strip(s6, [-1.6, 0.0, 1.3, 3.2],
                 ["−1.6 s · motion: the tight end goes left", "Snap · three to the left; one safety deep",
                  "+1.3 s · caught behind the line; five rushing", "+3.2 s · sixteen yards after the catch"],
                 lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 18.0))
```

Why does a screen beat a blitz? Because every extra rusher is a defender who isn't covering anyone, and a
screen deliberately lets the rushers through to put the ball where they came from. A pressure call against a
screen is the worst outcome for a defense, and it happens because the defense was guessing too: second-and-1
from the shotgun is a coin flip for everyone. This is the snap where step 8 earns its place. If you'd seen a
linebacker creeping toward the line and counted only one safety deep, your second-layer call would have moved
from "four rush" toward "five or more, ball out fast", and the base rate would have been wrong for a reason
you could see.

**Snap 7: first-and-10 at the Rams' 20.** Back to 12 personnel, under center, two backs, motion, against base
and a seven-man box. Every step says run: `{python} snap_conf(7)`. It was play-action. Darnold faked the
handoff, left the pocket and, after 4.7 seconds, found the tight end AJ Barner short on the left for seven. ✗.
This is the miss you *should* have, the tendency-breaker built to beat the reader who believes the look: an
offense from the Shanahan tree lives on making its run and play-action looks identical
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). At
`{python} int(D.loc[7, "conf"])`% the call was honest. At 95% it would have been a misread.

**Snap 8: second-and-3 at the 13, no huddle.** Seattle hurried to the line in the same personnel, under center
with one back. The call is `{python} snap_conf(8)`, and it missed again: a quick throw to Jake Bobo, out 0.6
seconds after the snap, incomplete. The second layer split: in this spot (second-and-short in the red zone,
four defensive backs) the 2025 base rates said man (`{python} int(D.loc[8, "cov_conf"])`%) and five or more rushers
(`{python} int(D.loc[8, "rush_conf"])`%). The Rams did send five, but played Cover 3 behind them. Two run-call misses
in a row, both passes from a run look, is not bad reading; it's a play-caller deliberately working against his
own tendency in the red zone. The between-snaps habit (line 13 on the card) is where you'd note it: *12
personnel under center, inside the 20, two passes in a row*. If they come back to it, your next call from that
look should drop toward 55%.

**Snap 9: third-and-3 at the 13.** Shotgun, 11 personnel, motion: the model says `{python} snap_conf(9)`.
Third-and-short in the red zone is one of the few spots where man coverage is about as common as zone (the 2025
base rate for this spot was man `{python} int(D.loc[9, "cov_conf"])`%), so the coverage call was close to a coin
flip. The Rams played zone, a Cover 6 (quarters to one side, Cover 2 to the other),
and rushed four. They got pressure, but Darnold threw on time, 2.4 seconds after the snap, to a receiver in his
progression rather than a checkdown:[^read] Kupp on a short post, caught at the 6, six more yards after the catch, touchdown. ✓

```{python}
#| label: fig-snap9
#| fig-cap: "Snap 9, third-and-3 at the Rams' 13 (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun with motion; nickel, six in the box; four rushers, with pressure; Cover 6; the ball thrown inside the progression (not a checkdown) to Cooper Kupp (H, ringed), on a post from the right side, seven yards in the air and six after the catch for the touchdown. Illustrative: the alignments, the tight end's motion (Y), the other routes, which rusher got home, and the coverage drawn as quarters on Kupp's side and Cover 2 on the other. Here the quarters safety on Kupp's side widens to help on the fade outside him and comes back too late. What to notice: in the red zone the deep defenders are already near the goal line, so a short post that gets inside the nickel and in front of the safety has room to run."
def snap9():
    off = offense("gun_2x2", strength="left")      # X wide right, H (Kupp) right slot, Y left slot, Z wide left
    dfn = [Player("WDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, -5.8), Player("WDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -2.0),
           Player("SDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, 1.0), Player("SDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 5.8),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.0, 1.5), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 4.0, -2.5),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 4.5, 7.4), Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 5.0, -15.8, label="CB"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 6.0, 15.8, label="CB"), Player("FS", "FS", "def", 10.0, -8.0),
           Player("SS", "SS", "def", 9.5, 7.0)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=97, to_go=3)
    p.highlight("H")
    p.motion("Y", to=(-1.5, -5.4), speed=5.0)                 # short motion in to a wing
    p.motion("WILL", to=(4.0, -3.4), speed=1.5)               # a bump, not a chase: zone
    # offense
    p.route("H", r.path((4.0, 0.0)), speed=5.0)
    p.route("H", r.path((0.5, 1.2)), speed=5.0)               # a jab outside...
    p.route("H", r.path((4.0, -3.2)), speed=5.0)              # ...then the post, inside the nickel
    p.route("H", r.path((0.6, -1.2)), speed=1.0)              # finds the window in front of the safety
    p.route("H", r.path((6.5, -1.5)), speed=6.5)              # and runs it in
    p.route("X", r.fade(14)); p.route("Z", r.slant(2, 6)); p.route("Y", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.4, 0.6)])
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    p.block("RT", pts=[(-1.4, 0.8), (-2.6, 0.6)], speed=1.5)   # beaten
    p.dropback(2.5)
    # defense: four rush; quarters to the right, Cover 2 to the left
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("SDE", pts=[(-2.5, 1.0), (-5.0, -4.8)], speed=3.9)  # the pressure arrives as the ball leaves
    p.drop("RCB", (12.0, 15.0), speed=4.5)
    p.drop("SS", (12.0, 10.5), speed=2.5)                      # #2 went inside: he helps on X's fade...
    p.path("SS", [(12.8, 7.0)], speed=4.5, delay=0.9, absolute=True)   # ...and comes back too late
    p.path("NB", [(5.5, 9.4)], speed=4.0, absolute=True)       # bites on the jab
    p.path("NB", [(9.5, 6.0)], speed=5.0, delay=0.6, absolute=True)
    p.drop("LCB", (3.0, -13.5), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -8.0), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -5.5)); p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 1.0))
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.4)
    return p


s9 = snap9()
animate_or_strip(s9, [0.0, 1.6, 3.3, 4.6],
                 ["Snap · after the motion: nickel, six in the box", "+1.6 s · Kupp jabs outside; the nickel bites",
                  "+3.3 s · caught at the 6, in front of the safety", "+4.6 s · touchdown"],
                 lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 22.0))
```

Add it up. The run-or-pass calls went `{python} N_HIT` for 9. The three misses were all passes from looks
that lean run: a coin flip on second-and-1, then play-action and a quick throw from under center with two tight
ends, the looks an offense uses to spend its tendency. On the `{python} N_PASS` dropbacks the second layer went
`{python} N_COV` for `{python} N_PASS` on the coverage family and `{python} N_RUSH` for `{python} N_PASS` on the
rush count. The coverage misses both came in the red zone, where the base rate leaned man and the Rams played
zone; the rush miss was the second-and-1 blitz. That's a realistic live result for a good reader, and it says
where the extra points are: in the red zone and on second-and-short, steps 4, 6 and 8 (the motion response, the
shell and the pressure tells) are worth more than the base rate, so look harder there before you trust it.

Three habits from the drive are worth keeping:

- **Score the read, not the play.** Snap 2 was a correct run call on a run that lost yards. Snap 3 was a
  correct pass call on a checkdown that only converted because of the yards after the catch. Your log grades
  you on what you could know before the snap.
- **Expect the tendency-breaker where it is cheapest.** Play-action from a heavy look on first down, and a
  quick pass from the same look in the red zone, are the classic places an offense spends a tendency. A 65%
  call that misses there is fine; a 90% call that misses there is a lesson.
- **Notice the defense's bets.** Dime with five in the box on third-and-9, a nickel against two tight ends on
  second-and-7, five rushers on second-and-1: each is the defense making its own prediction, and each is a
  clue to the second layer.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the same drive in real tracking data"}
The figures above are simulations in the Big Data Bowl's tracking format, built from the charting. The NFL
releases real player-tracking data only for the seasons and weeks of each year's Big Data Bowl, and no public
release covers the 2025 playoffs (the 2026 edition used the 2023 regular season). For a play that is in a
release, the real version is one call to `gridiron.bdb.prepare()` away (the code is in the web version of this
page), and [Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
walks through it.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")     # a Big Data Bowl release, downloaded from Kaggle
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
```

## Between snaps: keeping the read up to date

The checklist is per-snap, but the best clue about the next snap is often the last twenty. Two habits keep
your read current, and both happen while the broadcast is doing something else.

**After every snap (five seconds, during the replay):** write the log line. The call, the confidence, the clue
that decided it, the result. That's line 12 on the card, and it's the habit [How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)
started. Don't skip the clue column: after a few games it tells you which tells are working *for you*.

**At every stoppage (a TV timeout, the end of a quarter, a change of possession):** update the picture of this
team, today. Three questions:

1. **What are they doing from each look?** "Three runs from 12 personnel under center on first down" is a
   game tendency. It is more current than any season number, and play-callers know it too, so expect the
   [tendency breaker](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-breaker) when the streak gets long. That's
   the honest version of the "they're due" instinct: not that a pass is owed, but that the play-caller is
   watching the same tally you are.
2. **What did they just change?** Staffs adjust between series, not just at halftime: a new protection
   against a rusher who is winning, a coverage rolled toward a receiver who is hurting them, a run that
   worked coming back with a twist ([In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)).
   The call after a successful play is often built on it.
3. **What does the clock want?** The score and the time left change the base rate before step 1 even starts:
   a team ahead late runs, a team behind throws, and inside the last two minutes of a half the clock rules from
   [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)
   take over. Fourth down is its own prediction: go, kick or punt, before the offense decides.

### When the offense goes fast

Against [tempo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tempo) the twenty seconds shrink to five or ten, and the full
checklist won't fit. Run the short one: **1, 3, 6, 9**. Situation (you already have it from the last snap,
plus the new down and distance), formation (the single biggest clue after the situation), shell (the single
most useful second-layer clue), and the call. Drop personnel (it usually hasn't changed; that's the point of
tempo), motion (tempo offenses use less of it), and the box and leverage counts you can't finish anyway. The
measured value of what you drop is small for run or pass; the cost is mostly in your second layer, so lower
those confidences when the offense is hurrying.

The same applies when the broadcast is still on a replay at the snap, which happens more than it should.
Call it from the situation alone, write "sit" as the clue, and move on. A 60% call from the scorebug is still
a call.

## The log, final form

Your log has grown a column at a time since Part 1. Here is its final form, the one
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) will score. Keep the columns from
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) (snap, quarter, clock, down,
to-go, ball on, score) and add or tighten these:

| Column | What you write | Example |
|:-------|:------------------|:-------------|
| `pers` | Offensive personnel, two digits | `12` |
| `align` | QB alignment and number of backs | `U1` (under center, one back), `S0` (empty) |
| `motion` | Motion or shift before the snap | `M` or blank |
| `box` | Defenders in the box, if you counted | `7` |
| `shell` | One-high or two-high, pre-snap | `1` or `2` |
| `call` | Run or pass | `R` |
| `conf` | Your stated confidence, as a decimal | `0.65` |
| `clue` | The one thing that decided it | `align` |
| `l2` | Your second-layer call | `zone`, `5+`, `left` |
| `l2conf` | Its confidence | `0.6` |
| `result`, `l2result` | What happened, filled in after the snap | `P`, `zone` |

At halftime, a few lines of pandas tell you how the half went. Here it is run on the drive above, saved as a
CSV the way you'd type it:

```{python}
#| echo: false
_log = pd.DataFrame({
    "snap": range(1, len(DRV) + 1), "down": DRV.down.astype(int), "togo": DRV.ydstogo.astype(int),
    "pers": DRV.pers, "align": DRV.qb_location + DRV.n_offense_backfield.astype(int).astype(str),
    "call": DRV.call.str[0], "conf": DRV.conf / 100, "clue": ["align"] * len(DRV),
    "result": np.where(DRV.is_pass, "P", "R")})
_cwd, _tmp = os.getcwd(), tempfile.mkdtemp()
_log.to_csv(os.path.join(_tmp, "nfc_title_q3.csv"), index=False)
os.chdir(_tmp)
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("nfc_title_q3.csv")
log["hit"] = log["call"] == log["result"]
print(f"Right on {log.hit.sum()} of {len(log)} calls ({log.hit.mean():.0%}); average stated confidence {log.conf.mean():.0%}")
bands = pd.cut(log.conf, [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.91], right=False, labels=["50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80-90"])
print(log.groupby(bands, observed=True).hit.agg(calls="size", right="mean").round(2).to_string())
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
os.chdir(_cwd)
```

Two numbers to watch over a season, not a half: your hit rate against your average stated confidence (if
you're right 70% of the time while claiming 80%, you're overconfident), and the hit rate within each band
(your 80% calls should come true about 80% of the time). Nine snaps can't tell you either; a few hundred can,
and that is what the next chapter does with them.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the live run"}
For **one half** of one game, watching one offense:

- **Before every snap**, run the card in order: situation, personnel, formation, motion response, box, shell,
  leverage, pressure, call. Say the call and a confidence between 50% and 90% out loud *before* the snap.
  If the broadcast is still on a replay, call it from the situation and write "sit".
- **On the snaps where you have time**, add one second-layer call with its own confidence: on likely passes,
  the coverage family or the rush (four, or five or more); on likely runs, the direction.
- **During the replay**, write the line: down, to-go, pers, align, call, conf, clue, and the second-layer
  call if you made one. Fill in the result.
- **At each stoppage**, update the tally of what this team does from each look today, and note anything it
  changed.
- **When the offense goes no-huddle**, switch to the short checklist (1, 3, 6, 9) and lower your second-layer
  confidences.
- **At halftime**, score it: hit rate, average confidence, and the hit rate of your 80%-plus calls. Keep the
  sheet. [Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) adds a second half of work to it: the All-22, the
  chart, and the score.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: first down, two backs"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-iform
#| fig-cap: "First quarter, 0–0. First-and-10 at the offense's own 30. The offense has 21 personnel (two backs, one tight end) in an I-formation: quarterback under center, fullback (F) and tailback (T) stacked behind him, the tight end (Y) on the right. The defense is in base with the strong safety (ringed) walked down to the edge of the box: eight defenders in the box, one safety deep in the middle."
off = offense("i_form")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
dfn = [p_.moved(d=6.5, w=7.4) if p_.key == "SS" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pd1 = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
pd1.highlight("SS")
fld = pd1.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.5, 17.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pd1, ["Q1  12:40", "0 – 0", "1st & 10, own 30"], at=(-7.2, -19.6))
tag(fld, pd1, "8 in the box", (8.8, 4.0), fs=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass, how sure are you, and if it's a pass, what kind?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Run, about 70%; and if it's a pass, expect play-action.** *Situation:* first-and-10 is a coin flip
(`{python} pct(RATE["first10"])` passes in 2025). *Personnel and formation:* 21 personnel with the quarterback
under center moves it a long way: on first-and-10 from that look, offenses threw only
`{python} pct(RATE["first21uc"])` of the time in 2025. *Box:* eight in the box with one safety deep is the
defense loading up against the run, and offenses facing it from this look threw a little *less* often
(`{python} pct(RATE["first21uc8"])`, though that's only `{python} N_FIRST21UC8` snaps).

So why not 85 or 90? Because this is the exact picture play-action is built for. One deep safety and eight
defenders committed to the run leave the deep middle and the space behind the linebackers thin, and an offense
that gets the linebackers to step up for the fake can throw a post or a deep crossing route behind them
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). The
I-formation also hides the run's direction: with the fullback straight behind the quarterback there's no
offset to read. A good log line: *call R, conf 0.70, clue align, l2 "if pass, PA shot"*.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the mugs on third down"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-mugs
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6 at the opponent's 42, second quarter. Shotgun, 11 personnel, two receivers each side, the back to the quarterback's left. The defense shows a pressure look: both inside linebackers (ringed) have walked up into the A gaps, either side of the center, so six defenders are at the line. Behind them, two safeties stand 12 yards deep and both corners are seven yards off."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
DM2 = {"MIKE": (1.0, 0.9), "WILL": (1.0, -0.9), "FS": (12.0, -9.0), "SS": (12.0, 9.0), "LCB": (7.0, -16.0),
       "RCB": (7.0, 16.0), "WDE": (1.0, -6.6), "WDT": (1.0, -2.6), "SDT": (1.0, 2.6), "SDE": (1.0, 6.6)}
dfn = [p_.moved(d=DM2[p_.key][0], w=DM2[p_.key][1]) if p_.key in DM2 else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pd2 = Play(off, dfn, los=68, to_go=6)
pd2.highlight("MIKE", "WILL")
fld = pd2.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pd2, ["Q2  6:15", "HOME 10 – AWAY 7", "3rd & 6, opp 42"], at=(-6.4, -19.6))
tag(fld, pd2, "two A-gap mugs", (3.6, -4.6), fs=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**It's a pass; how many will rush, and where should the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Pass, near certain; four rushers is still the best single call (about 60%), and the ball should come out
fast.** Run or pass is the cheap part: on third-and-4 to 6 from the shotgun with 11 personnel, offenses threw
`{python} pct(RATE["third46gun11"])` of the time in 2025. Spend the rest on step 8.

*Count the deep players first.* Two safeties at 12 yards and two corners seven yards off are four defenders
who are, for now, playing coverage. That leaves seven for the rush and the underneath zones, and six of them
are standing at the line. If all six rushed, there would be one defender underneath, which almost no defense
risks with the ball at midfield. So the realistic menu is: both mugs drop and four rush (a
[simulated pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-simulated-pressure), the creeper of
[Zone Blitzes](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)); one mug comes and one drops; or a
five-man pressure with a safety rotating down. On third-and-4 to 6 in 2025, defenses sent five or more on only
`{python} pct(RUSH["third46"])` of dropbacks. A pressure look moves that number up, but probably not past
half, so "four rush, 60%" is an honest call, and "five or more, 40%" is the alternative you keep in mind.

*Where the ball goes:* the offense has to protect against six, so the quarterback will likely set the
protection to the mugs and have a quick answer built in. Expect a throw in under 2.5 seconds, near the sticks,
to the side a dropping linebacker has the farthest to run to. And if a mug drops into the throwing lane, that
is the zone blitz doing its job.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: tempo after a first down"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-tempo
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-2 at the opponent's 45, third quarter. The offense just ran for 8 yards on first down out of 11 personnel and sprinted to the line without huddling or substituting. The defense, which had its base personnel on the field (three linebackers, two corners, two safeties), couldn't substitute: the strongside linebacker (ringed) has had to walk out over the slot receiver on the right."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
DM3 = {"SAM": (5.0, 8.4), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.0), "WILL": (4.5, -3.2), "FS": (12.5, -9.0), "SS": (12.5, 9.0),
       "LCB": (7.0, -16.0), "RCB": (7.0, 16.0)}
dfn = [p_.moved(d=DM3[p_.key][0], w=DM3[p_.key][1]) if p_.key in DM3 else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pd3 = Play(off, dfn, los=65, to_go=2)
pd3.highlight("SAM")
fld = pd3.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pd3, ["Q3  9:02", "HOME 17 – AWAY 17", "2nd & 2, opp 45  ·  no huddle"], at=(-6.4, -19.6))
tag(fld, pd3, "base defense, frozen", (9.0, -3.0), fs=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**What is the offense hunting, and what's your call?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A lean to pass, about 60%, aimed at the linebacker on the slot.** *Situation:* second-and-2 is a run
down overall (only `{python} pct(RATE["second12"])` passes in 2025), but from the shotgun with 11 personnel
it was `{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11"])`, and with no huddle `{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11nh"])` (a
small sample, `{python} N_SECOND12NH` snaps, so don't lean on the decimal). Second-and-short is also the down
where offenses take shots, because a failure still leaves third-and-short.

*Personnel and tempo:* this is the [substitution freeze](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-freeze)
at work. Because the offense didn't substitute, the defense had no guaranteed chance to swap a linebacker for a
nickel back, so its strongside linebacker is now covering a slot receiver in space. That is the matchup the
offense sprinted to the line to get: a quick throw or a crossing route at the linebacker, or a deeper shot if
the safeties cheat up for the run.

*Why only 60%:* the same frozen base defense has only six in the box, and with the tight end split out as a
slot the offense has five linemen to block them; a shotgun run in which the quarterback reads one defender
instead of blocking him evens that count. A team that just gained eight on the ground may simply run it again. Tempo tells you the offense likes
something about this picture; it doesn't tell you which of the two things it likes. A good log line: *call P,
conf 0.60, clue tempo, l2 "target the slot", 0.55*.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Order beats speed.** The master checklist asks nine questions in the order the game answers them
  (situation, personnel, formation, motion response, box, shell, leverage, pressure, call), and each answer
  changes what the next clue means.
- **Run or pass is mostly settled by step 3.** In 2024–2025 data the situation and the formation did almost all
  the work; motion, tempo and the box added under a point. Spend the later steps on the second layer: coverage,
  rush, where the ball goes.
- **Tells are leans with reasons.** Every tell in the catalogue leaks because of physics or assignment, and
  every one is broken on purpose by somebody. Trust them in proportion to how often they're right, and expect
  the break where it's cheapest for the offense.
- **Say a number.** A stated confidence between 50% and 90%, made before the snap, turns watching into
  something you can score. Start from the base rate, move with strong clues, and rarely go past 90.
- **Score the read, not the play.** A correct call on a failed play is a correct call, and a 65% call that
  misses on a tendency-breaker is honest reading.

[^clock]: NFL Football Operations, "Football terms" glossary (the 40-second play clock, and the 25-second clock after certain administrative stoppages): https://operations.nfl.com/learn-the-game/nfl-basics/terms-glossary/

[^radio]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules*, Rule 5, Section 3, Article 3 ("Speakers in helmets"): coach-to-player communication "is cut off when the play clock reaches 15 seconds or the ball is snapped, whichever occurs first." Rulebook: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . The rule and its history are covered in [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd).

[^gawande]: Atul Gawande, *The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right* (Metropolitan Books, 2009), on aviation checklists and the surgical safety checklist, and on the difference between "do-confirm" and "read-do" checklists; the watching checklist is the do-confirm kind, run from memory and checked against the card.

[^rates]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (quarterback alignment, tempo) and participation (personnel), 2025 regular season, runs and dropbacks with a down recorded. "Pass" is nflverse's `pass` flag, so sacks and scrambles count as passes, as in your log.

[^motion]: Daire Carragher, "NFL pre-snap motion usage reaches new highs across the NFL," PFF (Feb. 23, 2026): https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-pre-snap-motion-usage-reaches-new-highs-across-the-nfl . PFF's series counts shifts and motion together and is not comparable with FTN's `is_motion` flag, which nflverse defines as motion "before or at the time of the snap."

[^twohigh]: NFL.com, "The coverage that turned the Seahawks into Super Bowl winners and is taking the NFL by storm" (Next Gen Stats): https://www.nfl.com/news/the-coverage-that-turned-the-seahawks-into-super-bowl-winners-and-is-taking-the-nfl-by-storm (two-high on 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018, 42.0% in 2025).

[^worth]: Course calculation. Nested logistic regressions (ridge-penalised, fitted with numpy) on nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation. Training set: 2024 regular-season runs and dropbacks; test set: all 32,813 2025 regular-season runs and dropbacks. Situation = down by distance (1, 2, 3, 4–6, 7–10, 11+ yards), field zone, score margin (five bands), last two minutes of a half, and fourth quarter by score; personnel = offensive personnel group from participation; formation = FTN `qb_location` by number of backs (`n_offense_backfield`, 0, 1, 2+); motion and tempo = FTN `is_motion` and `is_no_huddle`; box = participation `defenders_in_box` (5 or fewer, 6, 7, 8+). nflverse's own `xpass` model, which uses only the situation, calls 71% of the same snaps correctly.

[^bands]: Same model and data as the chart of what each step is worth, using steps 1 to 3 only. Confidence is the model's probability for whichever side it called.

[^tetlock]: Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner, *Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction* (Crown, 2015), on the forecasting tournaments in which forecasters who used fine-grained numerical probabilities, kept score and updated often were more accurate.

[^cov]: Course calculation from nflverse participation (`defense_man_zone_type`) and FTN charting (`n_pass_rushers`), 2025 regular-season dropbacks with a rush count recorded; coverage share among those charted man or zone. On the season-to-season jumps in FTN's man share (28.8% in 2022 under the earlier NGS source, then 41.2%, 48.3% and 30.8% for 2023–2025), see the course's notes on the 2022/2023 source break in [Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).

[^nfc]: Score, date and site from nflverse schedules and play-by-play (game `2025_21_LA_SEA`: Seattle 31, Los Angeles Rams 27, January 25, 2026, Lumen Field); also "2025–26 NFL playoffs," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_NFL_playoffs . Seattle's 14–3 record and NFC top seed, and Super Bowl LX (Seattle 29, New England 13, February 8, 2026): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX .

[^staff]: Seattle's 2025 staff (Macdonald head coach, Kubiak offensive coordinator, Aden Durde defensive coordinator) as listed for Super Bowl LX: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Seattle_Seahawks_season and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX . For 2026, Kubiak became the Raiders' head coach and Brian Fleury is Seattle's offensive coordinator. Seattle signed Sam Darnold on March 13, 2025, and Cooper Kupp, released by the Rams, on March 14, 2025 (three years, about $45 million): https://www.si.com/nfl/cooper-kupp-signs-seahawks-rams-release ; both names appear on Seattle's snaps in the game's play-by-play.

[^drive]: nflverse play-by-play (`desc`, down, distance, yard line, `air_yards`, `yards_after_catch`), participation (`offense_personnel`, `defense_personnel`, `defenders_in_box`, `defense_coverage_type`, `defense_man_zone_type`, `time_to_throw`, `was_pressure`, `route`) and FTN charting (`qb_location`, `n_offense_backfield`, `is_motion`, `is_no_huddle`, `is_play_action`, `is_screen_pass`, `n_pass_rushers`, `n_blitzers`, `read_thrown`, `is_qb_out_of_pocket`), game `2025_21_LA_SEA`, Seattle's drive beginning at 9:41 of the third quarter. Charting is done by people and contains errors; the labels are FTN's, not the teams'.

[^read]: FTN's `read_thrown` field records which read in the quarterback's progression the ball went to, with "CHK" for a checkdown, "DES" for a designed throw with no progression (screens, many RPOs) and "SD" for a scramble drill; snaps 3, 5 and 7 of this drive are coded CHK, snaps 6 and 8 DES. This touchdown is coded "1". The nflverse data dictionary (https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html) says "0" is the first read and "1" the second, but in the 2025 file "0" appears on almost every run and on only about 2% of passes with air yards recorded, while "1" is by far the most common code on those passes (over half), which suggests "1" is in practice the primary read. Either way, it was a read in the progression, not a checkdown or a designed throw.
